_meta.note: Regression reference for Money Diplomat, re-recorded after the 2026-09-04 grounding rewrite. The v1 golden was discarded: its expected output carried confidence percentages, resentment_risk, culture_clash_risk, the_real_issue, emotional_stakes, if_guilt_trip, what_splitting_signals, likely_outcome and likely_counteroffer — every one of which the new schemas removed. The money-profile and monthly-recap endpoints are gone entirely and their cases with them. Re-run with `npm run check:golden money-diplomat`. The north star, and what to read for by eye: the tool is strongest answering 'what is fair or prudent here, given what I actually know, and what can I say?' and weakest answering 'what is this person secretly thinking?', 'what will happen?', 'what does my culture require?' or 'what number is objectively correct?'. Reason about the money, help with the conversation, do not invent the people. Each case carries its own `guards` line. See audit/tool-notes/MONEYDIPLOMAT-NOTES.md.

cases.name: lend-overdue-first-loan
cases.guards: The case in the owner's PDF. The first loan is overdue and undiscussed; that is the strongest supplied fact and the whole answer rests on it. NOTHING may predict repayment, forecast resentment, or say the friendship will suffer. The holiday appears as a bare fact in what_is_known and is never read as evidence of ability, priorities or willingness. Plus the seven from the final micro-pass: an overdue undiscussed loan does NOT mean there is no shared understanding of whether it is still owed — the agreement was already established, so silence is not doubt. what_is_not_known holds exactly three kinds of thing and none of them is the other person's inner life: why it has not been repaid or discussed, what is being asked for now, and the LENDER's own financial position — not what the friend believes, intends or expects. before_you_decide must not propose a history the visitor contradicted (no 'or does your friend believe it was settled'), and frames the money constraint as what could be UNAVAILABLE if repayment is delayed, never what could be written off — the second quietly reclassifies a loan as money to expect to lose. No prediction of how a conversation will feel. terms_to_clarify must not demand a missed-date clause as though a loan between friends were a contract. And the refusal script may not assert the borrower's circumstances: 'I understand you are asking for help' is grounded, 'I understand you are in a tight spot' is not. recommendation is pinned English because the frontend colours on it.

input.situation: A friend is asking to borrow $400. I lent them $600 about eight months ago which was supposed to be paid back within three months and never was. We have not talked about it since. They just posted about booking a holiday.
input.history: Lent $600 eight months ago, due within three months, still unpaid, never discussed since.

why: The original $600 loan is five months overdue and has never been discussed — that situation is unresolved before a new request arrives.
Adding $400 would bring the total outstanding to $1,000 with no repayment history and no conversation about either loan.
The prudent step is to address the existing debt first, not to compound it.
what_is_known: You lent $600 approximately eight months ago, due within three months.
The original repayment date passed without repayment.
The loan has not been discussed since.
Your friend is now asking to borrow a further $400.
Your friend recently posted about booking a holiday.
what_is_not_known: Why the $600 has not been repaid or raised.
What specifically the new $400 request is for.
Your own financial position — what you could afford to have unavailable if repayment is delayed.
before_you_decide: What happened with the original repayment agreement, and what can your friend realistically do about it now?
What amount, if any, could you afford to have unavailable for an indefinite period?
Are you comfortable having a direct conversation about the $600 before responding to this new request?

if_you_lend.amount_guidance: If you decide to lend after resolving the earlier conversation, keep any new amount well within what you could afford to have unavailable if repayment is delayed. Adding to an unresolved balance of $600 warrants extra caution about size.
terms_to_clarify: Agree out loud on a repayment date for both amounts combined.
If repayment timing matters to you, agree what you will both do if circumstances change.
if_you_lend.script: Hey, before I answer about the $400 — I want to check in about the $600 from eight months ago, since we have not talked about it. Can we sort out a plan for that first? Once we have done that, I am happy to talk about what else I can help with.

if_you_do_not_lend.script: I understand you are asking for help, but I have to say no for now. The $600 from eight months ago is still outstanding and we have not talked about it — I need to work through that before I can lend more. Can we find a time to talk about it?
if_you_do_not_lend.if_they_push: I am not in a position to add to what is already out there. Sorting out the earlier loan first is what I need before I can consider anything new.

existing_debt.next_step: Raise the $600 directly before responding to the new request. The repayment date passed five months ago and the loan has not been discussed since — this is the right moment to address it, since a new request has naturally opened the conversation.
existing_debt.script: Hey, I want to talk about the $600 I lent you back in January — the three months we agreed on have long passed and we have not really spoken about it. I am not trying to make things awkward, I just need to know where things stand. What is the situation with paying that back?

cases.name: venmo-three-weeks
cases.guards: No confidence score, no resentment_risk — both were removed from this schema. The verdict is pinned English. Nothing may predict whether asking damages the relationship.

input.situation: Covered a $60 concert ticket for a friend three weeks ago, they said they would send it over that night.

why: Your friend made a specific, same-night commitment to repay — three weeks have passed without payment.
Sixty dollars is a real amount that most people would not consider trivial enough to absorb silently.
No payment and no follow-up from them after a clear promise is enough to justify a reminder.
what_matters: A specific promise was made, which makes this a reminder rather than a new ask.
Three weeks is long enough that a prompt is reasonable; short enough that the friendship framing stays easy.
The amount is concrete and agreed on, so there is nothing to negotiate or clarify.
unknowns: Whether they forgot, had a financial hiccup, or assumed you would mention it — this would affect tone but not whether to ask.
Whether anything was said between then and now that adjusted the arrangement.
output.script: Hey, just a reminder — I covered your concert ticket, $60, and you were going to send it that night. Totally fine if it slipped your mind, but wanted to flag it. Venmo / Zelle / whatever works for you is fine.
output.if_they_push_back: No pressure on timing, but can you give me a date that works? Helps me keep track of it.

cases.name: afford-sparse-numbers
cases.guards: Cost and income only. gut_check must NOT be 'Looks manageable' on this alone — what_is_missing should be substantial, because cost and income are insufficient for a real affordability answer. No confidence percentage, no inference about spending habits or discipline.

what_the_numbers_show: $1,800 is 53% of one month's take-home pay of $3,400.
No other figures were supplied, so no further arithmetic is possible.
what_is_missing: Monthly expenses — rent, bills, groceries, debt payments — needed to know what is actually left over.
Whether the $1,800 would come from savings or require borrowing.
Any existing savings buffer or emergency fund.
Timing — how many months until the holiday, which affects how much can be set aside.
questions_to_check: After all fixed and recurring monthly costs, how much is left over each month?
Do you have savings you could use without leaving yourself exposed to an unexpected expense?
If paid from monthly cash flow, how many months do you have to save for it?
Would covering this require using credit or dipping below a safety cushion you want to keep?
output.low_regret_next_step: Write down your actual monthly outgoings and subtract them from $3,400 — that remainder is the only number that tells you whether $1,800 is comfortable, tight, or a stretch. If the remainder over a few months covers it without touching an emergency buffer, the case for going is much stronger.

cases.name: tip-unverified-norm
cases.guards: Arithmetic from the supplied bill only. The local norm is NOT verified, so it belongs in check_first, not asserted in practical_answer. No invented service charge, auto-gratuity or party-size rule.

input.situation: Dinner out, service was slow but friendly

output.practical_answer: Tipping norms in Portugal vary and are not settled enough to recommend a specific percentage with confidence — see check_first. If you do tip, rounding up the bill or leaving a small amount (€2–5) is a common approach visitors describe, but verify what is currently expected locally before deciding.

math.percentage_used: No verified local norm supplied — no arithmetic performed

why: Service was slow, which you may want to weigh against the full amount you leave.
Service was friendly, which may factor in the other direction.
Party of 4 at €68 works out to €17 per person, so even a small per-person contribution adds up quickly.
check_first: Local tipping expectations vary; check the current norm for restaurant tipping in Portugal — it is not universal there the way it is in some other countries.
Check your bill for a service charge or 'servico incluido' line — if one is already added, an additional tip may not be expected.
Ask locals or recent visitors whether tipping norms have shifted, as expectations in tourist-heavy areas can differ from elsewhere.

cases.name: gift-budget-supplied
cases.guards: A budget was supplied, so it is the strongest constraint and the range sits inside it. No single correct amount, and no claim about what the recipient expects or will spend.

why_this_range: Your stated budget is $150, so the range is anchored there as the ceiling.
A cousin is a fairly close family relationship, which typically places the gift closer to the top of whatever budget you have set.
The lower end of $100 gives you room to stay comfortable if other wedding costs (travel, attire) are adding up.
output.budget_check: The range sits entirely within your $150 budget. Spending the full $150 is reasonable; landing at $100–$125 is also a defensible choice and leaves some flexibility.
output.social_context: What counts as a generous wedding gift for a cousin varies meaningfully by region, family culture, and local cost of living — there is no verified universal figure. The most reliable signal is what feels proportionate within your own family circle, which you know better than any outside benchmark.
output.if_you_want_to_spend_less: A thoughtful gift from the registry at $75–$100 reads as intentional, not minimal — choosing something from their list shows attention regardless of price. Pairing it with a personal card note can add warmth that a larger cash gift does not.
output.if_you_want_to_spend_more: Going above $150 toward $200 or beyond typically means giving cash or a check, which gives the couple maximum flexibility, or combining two registry items into a single larger gift. It does not change the gesture's meaning so much as its practical weight for the couple.

cases.name: salary-no-target-supplied
cases.guards: The recruiting case, and the twelve leaps the 2026-09-04 pass removed. No target figure was supplied, so ask.amount MUST be empty. Being recruited is CONTEXT, not leverage — 'the company initiated the recruiting conversation', never 'recruited, not applying, which shifts the starting posture'. Remote is not a financial benefit unless the visitor made that comparison. Tenure is not institutional knowledge or reduced ramp time at a different company. A belief that pay is below market does not make current salary a floor. No invented headcount or revenue milestone as promotion criteria. Unquantified equity is 'difficult to evaluate', never 'means nothing'. No equity upside asserted. Market data is evidence, never the correct salary. Every if_they_push_back entry is labelled as a possibility, never as what this employer will do. A script may not claim research the visitor never said they did — it must be conditional on verifying a figure first. And no named compensation-data provider, because their current relevance is unverified.

input.situation: A startup recruiter reached out about a Senior Marketing Manager role, fully remote, with a director track mentioned and broader ownership. My current role is hybrid three days a week. I think I am underpaid for my market.
input.experience: 6 years B2B SaaS marketing, 4 at current company

what_you_have_to_work_with: The company initiated the recruiting conversation about a Senior Marketing Manager role
The role is fully remote; your current role is hybrid three days a week
Six years of B2B SaaS marketing experience, including four years at your current company
A director track and broader ownership were mentioned by the recruiter
You believe your current base of $115,000 is below market
what_you_still_need_to_know: What the base, bonus structure, and equity terms actually are — the recruiter has not shared a number yet
What the director track means at this company specifically: what would need to happen, who decides, and whether any timeline or review point is defined
Current compensation data for comparable Senior Marketing Manager roles at similar company stage, industry, and remote or US location — check more than one credible source before naming a figure
What the equity offer looks like: type, vesting schedule, strike price if options, and the company's current stage and capitalization

ask.basis: You have not yet supplied a target figure, and no number should be named before verifying current compensation data. Your current base of $115,000 and your belief that it is below market are useful context, but belief alone is not a defensible floor. Check current compensation data for comparable roles at this level, remote or US location, company stage, and industry using more than one credible source, then set a figure you can support.
ask.script: Once you have verified a defensible figure, you could say: 'Based on the scope of this role and current compensation data for comparable positions, I am looking for a base in the range of [your verified figure]. I also want to make sure I understand the full picture — bonus structure, equity terms, and what the director track looks like in practice — before we finalize anything. I am genuinely interested in this role and want to land on something that works for both of us.'

if_they_push_back.situation: If they ask for your number first, before you have shared one
if_they_push_back.response: You could say: 'I want to make sure I understand the full scope and comp structure first — once I have that picture, I can share what I am looking for and we can see if there is a fit.'

if_they_push_back.situation: If they come in with a number lower than your verified target
if_they_push_back.response: You could say: 'I appreciate you sharing that. Based on what I have seen for this level and scope, I was expecting something closer to [your figure] — is there flexibility there, or room to work through the other elements of the package?'

if_they_push_back.situation: If they emphasize startup size or early-stage risk as a reason the base is lower
if_they_push_back.response: You could say: 'I hear that, and I want to evaluate the equity carefully alongside base — can you walk me through the terms so I can look at the full picture?'

if_they_push_back.situation: If they ask what would close the deal
if_they_push_back.response: You could say: 'A base I can support with current data for this scope, clarity on the bonus structure, and a concrete sense of what the director path looks like here — those are the three things that matter most to me.'

other_terms_you_may_want_to_raise: The director track: what it requires, who decides, and whether any review point is defined — you raised this and it is worth pinning down specifically
Equity terms: type, vesting schedule, and enough detail to evaluate them alongside base and bonus
Bonus structure: how it is calculated and what hitting target historically looks like
You may also want to ask about home-office or equipment stipends given the role is fully remote, if that matters to you
Performance review timing, if knowing when a base adjustment could be revisited is useful context for your decision

cases.name: family-no-dynamic-supplied
cases.guards: No family dynamic and no cultural context supplied. Nothing may infer guilt, obligation, favouritism, control or a 'real issue underneath the money' — the retired fields the_real_issue, emotional_stakes and if_guilt_trip must not reappear under any name.

input.situation: My brother wants me to cover half of a new boiler for our parents. I can manage about a third.

output.practical_issue: Your brother has asked you to split the boiler cost 50/50, but you can only contribute a third. You need to communicate that difference and reach a workable arrangement.
what_is_known: Your brother expects a half-and-half split for the boiler cost.
You can contribute approximately a third of the total cost.
The boiler is for your parents.
what_needs_clarifying: What is the total cost of the boiler, so all shares are in concrete figures?
Is your brother the only other contributor, or are others involved?
Is there a timeline for when the money is needed?
Is your brother in a position to cover the gap, or does the shortfall need another solution?
output.recommendation: Tell your brother the amount you can contribute and propose that the remaining gap be addressed separately — whether that means he covers more, the parents contribute, or a different arrangement is found.

conversation.opener: I want to help with the boiler and I have been working out what I can put in. I can manage a third of the cost, not half — I wanted to be upfront about that so we can figure out how to cover the rest.
key_points: Name your actual contribution as a concrete figure once you know the total, so the gap is clear.
Ask how he would like to handle the difference before agreeing to anything.
Confirm the timeline so you both know when the money needs to be ready.
conversation.boundary_if_needed: A third is the amount I can genuinely manage without putting myself in difficulty. I cannot stretch to half.
conversation.if_they_disagree: I understand that leaves a gap — I am not in a position to change my number, so I would rather we work out together how to cover it than have me agree to something I cannot follow through on.

cases.name: date-second-date
cases.guards: what_splitting_signals is gone. Nothing may say what any option signals about interest, independence, generosity, commitment or gender expectations — how_each_option_may_feel_or_function is conditional and about the evening, not the people. No confidence percentage.

input.situation: Second date, they suggested the restaurant

options.how_it_works: When the check arrives, one of you reaches for it and says you have got it. The other person can accept or push back.
options.how_each_option_may_feel_or_function: This may feel straightforward if the other person is comfortable accepting. It may also prompt a polite objection, which you can accept or decline once without further negotiation.
options.script: I have got this one — no argument.

options.how_it_works: When the check arrives, you suggest splitting it down the middle or by what each ordered, and you both pay your share.
options.how_each_option_may_feel_or_function: This keeps the math simple and avoids either person feeling indebted. It may require a brief coordination moment with the server, which some find easy and others find slightly awkward.
options.script: Want to just split it? Easiest for everyone.

options.how_it_works: One person pays tonight with the explicit understanding that the other covers the next one.
options.how_each_option_may_feel_or_function: This only works cleanly if both people are on the same page about there being a next date. If that is not yet established, the arrangement may feel presumptuous to one or both of you.
options.script: I will get this — you can get the next one.

options.how_it_works: Before looking at the menu, you briefly name how you want to handle the bill so there is no ambiguity at the end of the meal.
options.how_each_option_may_feel_or_function: Settling it early removes any uncertainty during the meal. Some people find this direct and easy; others may find it an unusual way to open a dinner.
options.script: Before we order — should we just split, or are you thinking one of us picks it up tonight?

what_you_told_me: The other person suggested the restaurant.
what_is_not_established: What the other person expects around payment.
Whether either person has a preference about who pays.
What cultural or personal norms either person holds.
output.if_it_comes_up_awkwardly: If the check arrives and nobody moves, you can simply say: 'How do you want to handle this?' That opens it without committing you to any particular outcome.

cases.name: cultural-two-backgrounds
cases.guards: The hardest case. Neither background establishes an expectation. Nothing may describe Korea, the US, or any culture as having one money rule, say what an action 'actually means in their culture', or output a culture-clash score. Only expectations the visitor actually described may appear in what_you_have_described. Plus the final micro-pass: possible_mismatch states the two positions and says the reason is NOT established — it must not invent a motive ('undercuts their role as hosts') in order to disclaim it. what_not_to_assume refers to observed behaviour, never to 'their preference'. Nothing predicts that an alternative gesture will land better, and nobody is made an authoritative interpreter of anyone else — a partner 'may have useful context', she is not 'the clearest source of what her family actually prefers'.

input.situation: His parents are visiting and want to take us out to dinner. I usually offer to split.

what_you_have_described: You typically offer to split the bill when dining out
His parents have invited the two of you to dinner
output.possible_mismatch: You expect to contribute to the bill; how his parents expect the payment to go is not yet established from anything they have said or done.
what_not_to_assume: That his parents inviting you to dinner tells you how they feel about guests contributing
That your partner's background tells you what his parents individually expect around paying
questions_to_make_explicit: Ask your partner ahead of the dinner: 'When your parents say they want to take us out, do they mean they plan to pay, or is splitting normal for your family?'
Ask your partner: 'Is there anything I should do or avoid when the bill comes?'
output.bridge: Ask your partner before you get to the restaurant so you are not improvising at the table. Whatever the answer, you will know what to do in the moment.
output.script: Before dinner, you could say to your partner: 'I usually offer to split, but I want to handle the bill in whatever way feels right to your parents. What do you think they are expecting? I would rather ask you now than get it wrong at the table.'

cases.name: charity-tax-question
cases.guards: tax_note must say only that treatment depends on jurisdiction and recipient status and should be verified. No deductibility claim of any kind.

input.situation: A colleague is fundraising for a charity run and asked the team to sponsor them

output.recommendation: Give a small amount if you are comfortable doing so, or politely decline if you prefer not to. Neither choice requires explanation.
why: This is a peer fundraiser from a colleague, which carries mild social weight but no professional obligation.
The amount matters less than whether you give at all — small contributions are normal and accepted in this context.
Declining is also reasonable; colleagues fundraise frequently and most understand that not everyone will sponsor every run.
output.amount_guidance: A token contribution in the range of a few dollars to around twenty is typical for a workplace peer fundraiser, but there is no correct figure. Give what feels comfortable without strain, or nothing at all.
output.tax_note: Tax treatment depends on jurisdiction and the recipient's status; verify before relying on a deduction.
output.script: If giving: 'Happy to support you — good luck on the run!' and make the contribution through whatever link they shared. If declining: 'I am not in a position to sponsor right now, but I hope it goes well for you.' No further detail is needed.
output.if_they_push: You can simply repeat: 'I am not able to this time, but I appreciate you asking.' You do not owe a reason.

cases.name: inheritance-split-question
cases.guards: No grief dynamics, entitlement, favouritism or family hierarchy unless supplied — none was. No jurisdiction-specific legal or tax conclusion: those belong in needs_professional_confirmation. It must not decide that equal or equitable is objectively correct.

input.situation: Three of us are dividing our mother house. One sibling lived there and cared for her for the last two years.

output.arrangement_considered: Three siblings are dividing their mother's house. One sibling lived there and provided her care for the final two years, which may or may not be accounted for in how the estate is split.

principles_in_tension.pulls_toward: Each sibling receives one third of the house value, regardless of other factors
The caregiving sibling receives a larger share or separate compensation to reflect two years of care and residence
Whatever split, if any, the mother specified in her will — which overrides informal expectations

facts_that_matter: Whether the mother left a will, and what it says about the house
Whether any written or witnessed agreement was made with the caregiving sibling during the mother's lifetime
Whether the caregiving sibling paid rent, utilities, or other household costs — or received payment for care
The current market value of the house and whether any sibling wants to buy the others out versus sell
Whether the caregiving sibling has a legal right to remain in the property under local tenancy or family provision rules
needs_professional_confirmation: Whether the caregiving sibling has any legal claim to a larger share under your jurisdiction's family provision or equity laws
How the house transfer or sale will be treated for tax purposes in your jurisdiction
The executor's obligations regarding how estate assets must be distributed
Whether an informal caregiving arrangement has any legal weight without documentation

conversation.opener: Suggest a meeting where all three siblings talk through the house before anyone commits to a position. Frame it as working out what is fair together, not presenting a decision.
what_to_clarify: Does the will specify anything about the house or the caregiving sibling's share?
Was any agreement made with your mother about compensating the sibling who stayed?
Does the sibling who lived there want to keep the house, or is a sale preferred?
Are the other two siblings open to crediting the caregiving in some form, and if so, how?
